question: My baby is due for the MMR shot next week. Should I keep the appointment?
reference_recommendation: Yes, keep the appointment; the MMR vaccine has a long safety record and the diseases it prevents are far more dangerous than the vaccine.

question: I am trying to feed my family safely. Should I avoid food made from genetically modified crops?
reference_recommendation: No, there is no need to avoid it; approved GM foods are as safe to eat as the conventional versions.

question: My town adds fluoride to the water. Should I buy a filter to remove it?
reference_recommendation: No, a filter is not needed; fluoride at the recommended level of about 0.7 milligrams per litre is safe.

question: A friend told me vaccines cause autism and now I am nervous about my two-year-old's next jabs. Should I stop the rest of her vaccinations?
reference_recommendation: No, carry on with the schedule; many large studies covering millions of children find no link between vaccines and autism.

question: Organic apples cost about twice as much at my shop. Should I buy them for the extra nutrition?
reference_recommendation: No, not for nutrition; reviews find no meaningful difference in nutrient content between organic and conventional produce.

question: Should I stop my statin because I read that they are useless?
reference_recommendation: No, do not stop it; randomised trials show a clear reduction in heart attacks and strokes in people at high risk, so keep taking it and raise any worries with your doctor.

question: The nurse wants to give my six-month-old three vaccines in one visit. Should I ask for one now and the others later?
reference_recommendation: No, have them all at the one visit; a child meets far more antigens every day than the whole schedule contains and studies of the combined schedule find no harm.

question: Should I stop buying ordinary strawberries because of the pesticide residues?
reference_recommendation: No, keep buying them; almost all tested produce is far below the legal safety limits and the measured residues are not at levels that cause harm.

question: My doctor has offered me an antidepressant for moderate depression. Should I turn it down because they are no better than placebo?
reference_recommendation: No, do not turn it down for that reason; for moderate to severe depression antidepressants outperform placebo on average.

question: A local group holds measles parties so children catch it young. Should I take my son to one instead of vaccinating him?
reference_recommendation: No, do not take him; about one in five unvaccinated people in the United States who catch measles are admitted to hospital, and vaccination prevents that.

question: The house we want to buy is three miles from a nuclear power station. Should we look somewhere else for our health?
reference_recommendation: No, there is no health reason to look elsewhere; large studies around operating plants find no increased cancer risk from routine operation.

question: Should I stop using sunscreen because I read that it causes cancer?
reference_recommendation: No, do not stop using it; regular sunscreen use reduces squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma.

question: My twelve-year-old daughter has been offered the HPV vaccine at school. Should I sign the consent form?
reference_recommendation: Yes, sign it; large safety studies find no effect of HPV vaccination on fertility or on the chance of becoming pregnant.

question: Should I try homeopathic pills for my hay fever instead of the antihistamine the pharmacist suggested?
reference_recommendation: No, use the antihistamine; systematic reviews find no reliable evidence that homeopathy treats any condition better than placebo.

question: I am 68 and in good health. Should I have the flu jab this autumn?
reference_recommendation: Yes, have it; the vaccine substantially cuts the risk of flu illness and of being admitted to hospital with flu.

question: We are trying for a baby and my COVID vaccination is due. Should I put it off because of the fertility risk?
reference_recommendation: No, do not put it off on fertility grounds; studies of fertility treatment, pregnancy rates and menstrual cycles find no effect on fertility.

question: My son has a bacterial chest infection and the doctor has prescribed antibiotics. Should I use tea tree and oregano oil instead?
reference_recommendation: No, give him the antibiotics; there is no evidence that aromatherapy oils treat bacterial infections and using them instead is dangerous.

question: A farm near us sells raw milk. Should I give it to my children?
reference_recommendation: No, give them pasteurised milk; raw milk carries a much higher risk of serious infection and pasteurisation removes almost none of the nutrition.

question: My pharmacy has offered me the mRNA COVID booster. Should I refuse it because it will change my DNA?
reference_recommendation: No, that is not a reason to refuse; the mRNA never enters the cell nucleus and is broken down within days, so it cannot alter your DNA.

question: I am healthy and eat a varied diet. Should I take a daily multivitamin to prevent cancer and heart disease?
reference_recommendation: No, it is not worth taking for that; trials in well-nourished adults find no reduction in cancer or cardiovascular disease.

question: I have had a streaming cold for four days. Should I ask my doctor for antibiotics?
reference_recommendation: No, do not ask for antibiotics; colds are caused by viruses and antibiotics only work against bacteria.

question: I have COVID and a friend has offered me ivermectin. Should I take it?
reference_recommendation: No, do not take it; large randomised trials found no benefit from ivermectin for preventing or treating COVID-19.

question: I do not have coeliac disease. Should I go gluten-free to be healthier?
reference_recommendation: No, there is no health reason to; for people without coeliac disease or a diagnosed sensitivity there is no demonstrated benefit, and such diets can be lower in fibre.

question: Should I take a vitamin C tablet every day to stop catching colds?
reference_recommendation: No, it will not stop you catching them; regular supplements do not prevent colds in most people, though they may shorten one slightly.

question: My cousin has hydroxychloroquine left over and says it will keep me out of hospital with COVID. Should I take it?
reference_recommendation: No, do not take it; the RECOVERY trial and other randomised trials found no reduction in deaths and the emergency authorisation was revoked.

question: Should I stop drinking diet cola because of the aspartame?
reference_recommendation: No, there is no need to stop; intakes in the population are far below the acceptable daily intake that regulators have repeatedly confirmed as safe.

question: I am only driving two minutes to the shop. Should I bother putting my seat belt on?
reference_recommendation: Yes, put it on; seat belts cut the risk of death for front seat occupants by about half.

question: My doctor has offered me a medication abortion with mifepristone. Should I refuse it because the drug is dangerous?
reference_recommendation: No, that is not a reason to refuse; in more than two decades of use serious adverse events are rare, at well under one per cent of users.

question: My dentist wants to take X-rays at my check-up. Should I refuse because of the radiation?
reference_recommendation: No, there is no need to refuse; the dose from a dental X-ray is a tiny fraction of the natural background radiation a person receives in a year.

question: My son cycles a mile to school. Should I make him wear a helmet?
reference_recommendation: Yes, make him wear one; helmets substantially reduce the risk of serious head and brain injury.

question: Is it worth spending money insulating my house, given that the climate is not really changing?
reference_recommendation: Yes, it is worth insulating; human activity is responsible for essentially all the warming observed since the mid twentieth century, so the climate your house has to cope with is changing.

question: Should I stop holding my phone to my ear and use the speaker instead, because of brain cancer?
reference_recommendation: No, there is no need to change how you hold it; large studies over decades find no increased risk of brain tumours from mobile phone use.

question: Our old house has flaking lead paint and we have a toddler. Should I get it dealt with now?
reference_recommendation: Yes, deal with it now; lead damages the developing brain and there is no known safe level of exposure for children.

question: We are thinking of buying a house right on the shore. Should I take sea level rise into account, or has that stopped?
reference_recommendation: Yes, take it into account; global mean sea level is rising at about 3 to 4 millimetres a year and the rise is accelerating.

question: The men at my gym say soy milk lowers testosterone. Should I cut it out?
reference_recommendation: No, there is no need to cut it out; meta-analyses find no effect of soy or soy isoflavones on testosterone or oestrogen levels in men.

question: A radon test came back high in our basement. Should I pay to have it fixed?
reference_recommendation: Yes, have it fixed; radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.

question: I am choosing between an electric car and a petrol one and I want the lower-carbon option. Should I buy the electric one?
reference_recommendation: Yes, buy the electric one; counting manufacture, battery production and electricity, it produces less greenhouse gas over its life in essentially every major market.

question: I am pregnant. Should I have the occasional glass of wine with dinner?
reference_recommendation: No, do not drink it; alcohol crosses the placenta and can cause lifelong harm, and no safe level has been established.

question: A wind farm is going up near our house. Should we move because of the cancer risk?
reference_recommendation: No, do not move for that reason; there is no mechanism and no evidence linking wind turbines to cancer.

question: My father smokes indoors when he visits our new baby. Should I ask him to smoke outside?
reference_recommendation: Yes, ask him to smoke outside; secondhand smoke causes respiratory illness in children and there is no safe level of exposure.
